title: Part 1
text: A year after the Minnesota frogs hit the news, the chemical explanation was failing. Then a young researcher named Pieter Johnson went looking in a different place.

title: Part 2
text: Instead of staying inside a laboratory, Johnson went straight into the ponds of Santa Clara County, California, where deformed frogs had also been found. He surveyed about thirty ponds.
nxt: He compared the water, the animals, and the exact places where deformed frogs appeared. This was patient field detective work.

title: Part 3
text: That is the power of going outside. A laboratory can test one chemical at a time, but a pond contains everything at once:

title: Part 4
text: A pattern emerged. Deformed amphibians turned up only in ponds that also held a certain kind of snail. That was a strange clue.
nxt: A chemical spill does not need a snail to do its damage.

title: Part 5
text: Then researchers looked closely at the deformed frogs and saw something startling. Around the pelvic region and the limb buds were clusters of tiny cysts.
nxt: Inside each capsule lived a microscopic parasitic flatworm. Its scientific name is Ribeiroia ondatrae.

title: Part 6
text: The culprit was not a chemical spill. It was not nuclear waste. It was a parasite.

title: Part 7
text: To understand how a worm this small could do this, you have to know that Ribeiroia is a trematode. That means it cannot live its whole life inside one animal.
nxt: It needs three different hosts to complete its cycle. Its journey begins at the bottom of a muddy pond, in a humble freshwater ramshorn snail.

title: Part 9
text: That raises a puzzle. If the parasite has been around for so long, why did the 1990s bring such a startling wave of deformities?

title: Part 10
text: Remember that question, because the answer involves farmers, fertilizer, and a lot of algae.
